title: From pyramid to hourglass: The new architecture of the CPA firm
author: Kyle Walters

dup.label: from pyramid to hourglass new architecture cpa firm

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Staffing structure: AI threatens both pyramid and pipeline
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that AI can compress the labor-intensive middle of a professional-services pyramid while preserving human roles grounded in experienced judgment and client relationships. It proposes an hourglass architecture for CPA firms, but does not address the cluster’s training-pipeline risk or establish that this transition is already occurring.
qs: ## Introducing the hourglass  If AI compresses the middle — the process-heavy, labor-intensive production layer —  but the top and bottom of the organization remain irreplaceable, then the pyramid is the wrong shape for the modern CPA firm.

They're the ones who look at the complete picture and tell the client: "Here's what you should do and here's why." This layer is defined by expertise, pattern recognition and professional judgment — things that require years of accumulated experience and are extraordinarily difficult to automate.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Walters supports the cluster’s central proposition through a CPA-firm analogue: AI is strongest on structured, repeatable production tasks, while contextual professional judgment remains human-led, requiring firms to redesign staffing and workflows around enduring client value rather than wholesale professional replacement. His evidence is primarily experiential and predictive, and he does not address verification or governance in depth.
qs: These are pattern-recognition tasks performed on structured data, and they're precisely what AI was built for.

These decisions require contextual understanding, risk tolerance assessment, and the kind of professional judgment that comes from years of seeing how decisions play out across dozens of similar situations.

kp.k: Client demand centers on enduring human value
kp.d: Walters argues that CPA-firm strategy should be organized around client needs that technology will not change: trustworthy judgment, accessible human service, accurate and timely work, and competent coordination. This is a strategic analogy drawn from Jeff Bezos's account of Amazon, not an empirical finding about clients.
qs: CPA firms need to ask the same question: What will our clients always want, regardless of what technology does?
Clients will always want trustworthy judgment, a human being who makes the process feel easy, and the confidence that someone competent is coordinating all the moving pieces.

kp.k: Traditional pyramids depend on labor arbitrage
kp.d: The author characterizes the traditional CPA firm as a pyramid with partners above a broad production workforce of managers, seniors and staff. Its economics depend on hiring workers at one rate, billing them at another and increasing revenue through a wider base performing labor-intensive processes.
qs: For decades, CPA firms have been built on the same organizational hierarchy model. It's shaped like a pyramid.
The wider the base, the more revenue the firm generates.
The business model is, at its core, labor arbitrage: hire people at one rate, bill them at a higher one and extract the spread.

kp.k: The pyramid optimizes process rather than client value
kp.d: Walters argues that the broad junior base arose because accounting production historically required extensive manual labor, not because clients valued the number of staff involved. Because the structure is tied to a changing production process, he considers it vulnerable to AI-enabled restructuring.
qs: But notice what the traditional pyramid structure is built around: process. It's not built around value.
The wide base at the bottom of the pyramid doesn't exist because clients want it. It exists because the work demanded it.
The pyramid, in other words, is built around something that will change. And it's changing right now.

kp.d: Based on his own experience rather than a cited study, Walters says AI is particularly capable at the process-heavy middle of accounting engagements, including document ingestion, data extraction, population, compliance checks, drafting and initial review. He reports that a discrepancy-review task formerly taking a second-year associate three hours can be performed by a model in seconds, but provides no benchmark, sample or measured accuracy.
qs: I have found AI to be exceptionally good at the work that lives in the middle of a typical engagement: ingesting a document, reading a W-2, a 1099 or a K-1 and extracting the data.
Data population, compliance checks and draft preparation are rapidly getting there.
Take the initial review that a second-year associate used to spend three hours on. A model can flag the same discrepancies in seconds.
These are pattern-recognition tasks performed on structured data, and they're precisely what AI was built for.

kp.k: Professional judgment remains difficult to automate
kp.d: The author predicts that AI will remain poor for a meaningful but unspecified period at nuanced tax and structuring decisions involving context, risk tolerance and tensions between short- and long-term interests. He attributes this work to experienced professionals whose judgment has developed across many comparable matters.
qs: What AI is not good at, and won't be good at for a meaningful period, are the things that sit at either end of the engagement.

These decisions require contextual understanding, risk tolerance assessment, and the kind of professional judgment that comes from years of seeing how decisions play out across dozens of similar situations.

kp.k: AI cannot replace client relationship work
kp.d: Walters asserts that models are not equipped to manage emotionally sensitive, explanatory and coordinative interactions, such as reassuring clients facing tax problems, advising distressed business owners or coordinating professionals during a divorce. He presents empathy, communication and service as enduringly human sources of client value.
qs: AI is also not equipped to handle the other side of the equation: human relationships.
It doesn't know how to handle a client who calls in a panic because they got a scary letter from the IRS.
No model handles this. And clients have never wanted it to.

kp.k: AI shifts firms from pyramids to hourglasses
kp.d: The central prediction is that AI will compress the process-heavy middle of CPA firms while leaving senior advice and client-facing relationship functions comparatively irreplaceable. Walters therefore proposes an hourglass staffing architecture rather than the traditional pyramid.
qs: If AI compresses the middle — the process-heavy, labor-intensive production layer —  but the top and bottom of the organization remain irreplaceable, then the pyramid is the wrong shape for the modern CPA firm.
The right shape is an hourglass.

kp.k: Senior professionals form the advice layer
kp.d: In the proposed hourglass, partners, senior advisors and experienced managers occupy the upper Advice Layer. They review AI-enabled output, exercise professional judgment and communicate recommendations, making human verification and reliance on accumulated expertise central to the model.
qs: The top of the hourglass is the Advice Layer.
They review the output, make the calls and deliver the advice.
This layer is defined by expertise, pattern recognition and professional judgment — things that require years of accumulated experience and are extraordinarily difficult to automate.
This is the trust layer.

kp.k: Client-facing staff form the relationship layer
kp.d: The lower Relationship Layer consists of client service associates and others who answer questions, collect documents, explain outcomes and maintain personalized follow-up. Walters argues that these roles persist because clients continue to value empathy, communication and a human service experience.
qs: The bottom of the hourglass is the Relationship Layer.
This is your client-facing team.
These are the people who make the process feel human.
This layer is defined by empathy, communication and service, skills that are fundamentally human and that clients will always value.

kp.k: AI narrows processing roles and junior staffing
kp.d: The narrow Processing Layer contains document ingestion, extraction, return population, compliance, workpaper generation and initial review. Walters predicts that models will perform work previously assigned to a broad base of staff and seniors, reducing the number of people needed for processing and specifically displacing work associated with second-year associates.
qs: The narrow middle of the hourglass is the Processing Layer. This is where AI lives.
It's all the work that used to require a wide base of staff and seniors grinding through files.
The hourglass pinches here in the middle because you simply don't need the same number of people doing processing work anymore.
The work still gets done. It just gets done by models, not by a bullpen of second-year associates.

kp.k: Firms should invest around enduring client needs
kp.d: Walters recommends accepting continued technological change and evaluating tools by whether they increase delivery of judgment, trust, responsiveness and human service. He frames this as a durable strategy that avoids tying organizational design to any particular AI tool.
qs: The technology in the middle will keep evolving. Don't try to stop it.

When you build your firm around the things that don't change, you stop worrying about what the next tool does and start asking the only question that matters: "How do we use it to deliver more of what our clients have always wanted?"

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Kyle Walters claims that AI increasingly performs CPA firms’ processing work, reducing the human staffing required and making an hourglass structure more appropriate than the traditional pyramid.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain argument about tax and accounting firms, not a claim about legal services. Walters describes the traditional pyramid as labor arbitrage supported by a large production workforce. He argues that AI can take over document ingestion, data extraction, return population, compliance checks, workpaper generation and initial review. His proposed hourglass retains an Advice Layer of partners, senior advisors and experienced managers and a Relationship Layer of client-facing service staff, while narrowing the Processing Layer. This is both a prediction about staffing requirements and a recommendation for organizational design; the article does not document a completed sector-wide transition.

pts.k: Walters claims substantial present-day processing capabilities and speed gains, while distinguishing some established capabilities from others still developing.
pts.d: He says AI already reads source documents, drafts returns and client communications, summarizes engagement letters and generates advisory memos. In his more qualified discussion, he describes document ingestion and extraction as particularly strong, with data population, compliance checks and draft preparation advancing toward that level. He claims a model can flag in seconds the discrepancies previously identified through a second-year associate’s three-hour initial review.

pts.k: Walters predicts continuing human importance in contextual professional judgment, review of output and client relationships.
pts.d: He distinguishes automatable production from decisions involving tax elections, entity structure, risk tolerance and competing short- and long-term objectives. He also claims AI cannot provide the relationship support clients need during stressful events. His model combines substitution for processing labor with retained human review and advice, rather than fully autonomous delivery. He recommends organizing around what he regards as enduring client demand for trustworthy judgment, competent coordination and human service.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is Walters’s practitioner experience, illustrative task comparisons and strategic reasoning, not a reported empirical study.
pts.d: Walters is identified as a partner at L&H CPAs and Advisors. He explicitly grounds his assessment of document-processing capabilities in what he has found in practice. The three-hours-versus-seconds comparison supplies a concrete illustration, but the article gives no named model, testing protocol, sample, accuracy results or independent benchmark. Claims about enduring limits on judgment and relationships are supported by examples and professional reasoning rather than measured evidence. His invocation of Jeff Bezos and Amazon is a strategic analogy for building around stable customer needs, not evidence of AI’s performance or CPA staffing outcomes; the CPA predictions are Walters’s.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Walters presents processing automation as already occurring in March 2026, further improvement as ongoing, and human judgment and relationship advantages as lasting for an unspecified period.
pts.d: The article was published on March 17, 2026. Present-tense claims coexist with the qualification that several processing capabilities are still developing. The hourglass argument is conditional on AI compressing production while advice and relationship functions remain human strengths. Walters gives no implementation deadline, staffing reduction percentage or defined duration for the phrase 'a meaningful period.' His claims about clients always valuing human service are stronger and more open-ended than that capability forecast. Hiring, talent development and investment implications are deferred to a promised second article.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Production staff face reduced staffing demand; experienced advisors retain judgment and review responsibilities; client-facing staff remain central; owners must reconsider firm design.
pts.d: The primary audience is CPA-firm owners and managing partners. Staff, seniors and second-year associates doing routine processing are the roles Walters identifies as most exposed to substitution. Experienced managers, senior advisors and partners occupy the retained Advice Layer, including human checking of output. Client service associates retain document collection, communication, follow-up and support responsibilities. Clients are presented as caring about accurate, timely work and trusted explanation rather than the number of staff involved. Although attorneys appear in an example of coordinating support during a divorce, Walters makes no separate claim about AI’s effect on lawyers or legal markets. He does not quantify employment losses, fee changes or client savings.
